subject: HSS
overview: World History 7 runs chronologically from late Rome to the Enlightenment across nine regions. Each week, add events to the wall timeline, use a map every few days, and read at least one primary source closely, asking who wrote it, when, why and for whom. Your child should answer in complete sentences with evidence and practice paragraph and DBQ writing (thesis, document evidence, explanation). Present religious beliefs descriptively and respectfully, as the CA framework requires.

weeks.prep: Long strip of paper for a 300–1800 CE wall timeline; blank Mediterranean map; Twelve Tables excerpt (Fordham Ancient History Sourcebook); cardboard, scissors and tape for the arch.
misconceptions: Thinking Rome 'fell' all at once and the whole empire ended. The western half fell in 476 CE; the eastern (Byzantine) half lasted until 1453.
Confusing the Roman Republic and Empire. The Twelve Tables come from the Republic (c. 450 BCE); the Empire began with Augustus (27 BCE).

days.guide: Lay out the timeline (1 cm or 1 inch per 10 years) and mark 476, 1054, 1215, 1492 and 1776 as anchors. On a world map your child locates the year's regions (Rome/Byzantium, Arabia, China, West Africa, Japan, Europe, Mesoamerica/Andes). Check before moving on: ask "How many years does the course timeline cover?" Look for: 1,500 years (300 to 1800 CE).

questions.q: How many years does the course timeline cover?

days.guide: Show a map of the empire under Trajan (117 CE, its greatest extent). Your child labels Rome, Constantinople, the Rhine and Danube frontiers, and provinces such as Gaul, Hispania, Britannia and Egypt. Check before moving on: ask "Why were the Rhine and Danube important?" Look for: They formed natural river frontiers that the army defended against Germanic peoples.

questions.q: Why were the Rhine and Danube important?
questions.a: They formed natural river frontiers that the army defended against Germanic peoples.

days.guide: Read selected laws aloud. Your child lists three ideas still in modern law (laws written and posted publicly, the right of the accused to appear in court, penalties for false testimony, property rights). Check before moving on: ask "Why did plebeians want laws written down?" Look for: So patricians (judges) could not interpret unwritten laws unfairly; written laws apply to everyone.

questions.q: Why did plebeians want laws written down?
questions.a: So patricians (judges) could not interpret unwritten laws unfairly; written laws apply to everyone.

days.guide: Show images of roads, aqueducts and the Pantheon. Your child builds a cardboard arch with a keystone and tests how much weight it holds. Check before moving on: ask "Why does an arch carry heavy loads?" Look for: The stones press against each other (compression), spreading the weight outward and down to the supports; the keystone locks them.

questions.q: Why does an arch carry heavy loads?
questions.a: The stones press against each other (compression), spreading the weight outward and down to the supports; the keystone locks them.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph on Rome's most important legacy, then takes the map and vocabulary quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Name three Roman legacies." Look for: Written law/legal ideas, Latin (root of Romance languages), engineering (roads, aqueducts, arches, concrete), republican government ideas.

questions.a: Written law/legal ideas, Latin (root of Romance languages), engineering (roads, aqueducts, arches, concrete), republican government ideas.

weeks.assessment_key: Map quiz: Rome, Constantinople, Rhine, Danube, Mediterranean, Gaul, Hispania, Egypt, Britannia. Vocabulary: republic, empire, citizen, aqueduct, legacy. Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence answering the prompt, at least two accurate specific facts or document references, explanation of how they support the claim, concluding sentence; 3 = accurate but thin explanation; 2 = general statements, few facts; 1 = off-topic or inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Cause-effect organizer; map of barbarian invasion routes; St. Jerome's letter (Letter 127 or 128, Fordham Sourcebook); five short documents on Rome's decline.
misconceptions: Picking one single cause. Historians see many interacting causes: political, economic, military and outside pressure.
Thinking 'barbarian' means uncivilized savages. Romans used it for non-Romans; many Goths were Christian and had served in Rome's army.

days.guide: Read a summary of 3rd–5th-century problems. Your child sorts causes into political, economic and military columns. Check before moving on: ask "Sort: inflation from debased coins; frequent civil wars; hiring Germanic mercenaries." Look for: Economic; political; military.

questions.q: Sort: inflation from debased coins; frequent civil wars; hiring Germanic mercenaries.
questions.a: Economic; political; military.

days.guide: Your child maps the routes of the Huns, Visigoths and Vandals and marks the sack of Rome. Check before moving on: ask "Who sacked Rome in 410?" Look for: The Visigoths under Alaric.

questions.a: The Visigoths under Alaric.

questions.q: When did the Western Empire end?
questions.a: 476 CE, when Odoacer deposed Emperor Romulus Augustulus.

days.guide: Read Jerome's reaction. Your child identifies his tone (shock, grief) and point of view (a Christian scholar living far away in Bethlehem). Check before moving on: ask "What does Jerome mean by 'the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken'?" Look for: Rome, which conquered so much, was itself conquered — showing his shock that the unthinkable had happened.

questions.q: What does Jerome mean by 'the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken'?
questions.a: Rome, which conquered so much, was itself conquered — showing his shock that the unthinkable had happened.

days.guide: Your child reads five documents, notes the cause each supports, and ranks causes with reasons. Check before moving on: ask "Example reasoning for ranking economic decline first?" Look for: Without money, emperors couldn't pay soldiers, so they relied on mercenaries and couldn't defend the borders.

questions.q: Example reasoning for ranking economic decline first?
questions.a: Without money, emperors couldn't pay soldiers, so they relied on mercenaries and couldn't defend the borders.

days.guide: Your child writes a 5-paragraph essay on the three most important causes with document evidence. Check before moving on: ask "What must the thesis do?" Look for: Name the three causes and argue they were the most important.

questions.a: Name the three causes and argue they were the most important.

weeks.assessment_key: Mini-DBQ essay rubric (4–1): Thesis names three causes; each body paragraph uses at least one document plus explanation; accurate facts (410 sack, 476 end, inflation, mercenaries, divided empire under Diocletian); conclusion; organization. Proficient = 3+ in each area.

weeks.prep: Map of Constantinople; Procopius excerpt on Theodora and the Nika riots (532); selections from Justinian's Code; Smarthistory video on Hagia Sophia; Venn diagram.
misconceptions: Thinking the Byzantines called themselves Byzantines. They called themselves Romans.
Thinking the Great Schism was only about religion. Politics and language (Greek vs. Latin) mattered too.

days.guide: Analyze the map. Your child explains three advantages of the location. Check before moving on: ask "Three advantages?" Look for: Water on three sides for defense, the Golden Horn harbor, control of the Bosporus trade route between the Black Sea and Mediterranean, and position between Europe and Asia.

questions.a: Water on three sides for defense, the Golden Horn harbor, control of the Bosporus trade route between the Black Sea and Mediterranean, and position between Europe and Asia.
Emperor Constantine.

days.guide: Read the Procopius passage. Your child evaluates his reliability. Check before moving on: ask "What does Theodora urge?" Look for: That Justinian not flee; she says royalty makes a good burial shroud, meaning she'd rather die an empress.

questions.a: That Justinian not flee; she says royalty makes a good burial shroud, meaning she'd rather die an empress.
He was a court historian who also wrote the 'Secret History' attacking Justinian and Theodora, so his accounts may be biased in different directions.

days.guide: Read selected laws. Your child compares them with the Twelve Tables. Check before moving on: ask "What was Justinian's Code?" Look for: A collection and organization of Roman law (529–534 CE) that became the basis of many European legal systems.

questions.a: A collection and organization of Roman law (529–534 CE) that became the basis of many European legal systems.

days.guide: Fill the Venn diagram. Your child explains the 1054 split. Check before moving on: ask "Two differences?" Look for: The pope claimed authority over all Christians, while Orthodox recognized patriarchs; Latin vs. Greek in worship; Orthodox priests may marry.

questions.a: The pope claimed authority over all Christians, while Orthodox recognized patriarchs; Latin vs. Greek in worship; Orthodox priests may marry.
The pope's representative and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, splitting Christianity into Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox.

days.guide: Give the unit 1 test. Then view Hagia Sophia mosaics and have your child write how art showed Byzantine power. Check before moving on: ask "How did mosaics show power?" Look for: Gold mosaics showing emperors beside Christ or Mary connected the emperor's power to God.

questions.a: Gold mosaics showing emperors beside Christ or Mary connected the emperor's power to God.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test: 1) 117 CE greatest extent. 2) Twelve Tables = written laws. 3) Arches/aqueducts. 4) 410 Visigoths, 476 fall of West. 5) Constantinople founded 330 on the Bosporus. 6) Justinian's Code organized Roman law. 7) Theodora's role in the Nika riots. 8) 1054 Great Schism. Short response on art proficient with a specific mosaic and its message.

weeks.prep: Physical map of Arabia; Khan Academy video on the origins of Islam; timeline paper; three-religion comparison chart.
misconceptions: Thinking Arabia was entirely empty desert. It had oases, towns and busy trade routes.
Confusing the hijra with the hajj. The hijra (622) was Muhammad's migration to Medina; the hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca.

days.guide: Your child maps the deserts, oases, Red Sea coast and caravan routes and compares Bedouin and town life. Check before moving on: ask "How did Bedouin live?" Look for: As nomadic herders moving with camels, sheep and goats between oases and pastures.

questions.a: As nomadic herders moving with camels, sheep and goats between oases and pastures.
Settled merchants and craftspeople in oasis towns like Mecca and Yathrib.

days.guide: Your child explains why Mecca was a crossroads. Check before moving on: ask "Why was Mecca important before Islam?" Look for: It was on caravan routes between Yemen and Syria and had the Kaaba, a shrine pilgrims visited.

questions.q: Why was Mecca important before Islam?
questions.a: It was on caravan routes between Yemen and Syria and had the Kaaba, a shrine pilgrims visited.

days.guide: Your child makes an illustrated timeline. Check before moving on: ask "Key dates?" Look for: 570 born in Mecca; 610 first revelation (Muslims believe from the angel Gabriel); 622 hijra to Medina (year 1 of the Islamic calendar); 630 returns to Mecca; 632 dies.

questions.a: 570 born in Mecca; 610 first revelation (Muslims believe from the angel Gabriel); 622 hijra to Medina (year 1 of the Islamic calendar); 630 returns to Mecca; 632 dies.

days.guide: Your child compares the three faiths. Check before moving on: ask "Shared beliefs?" Look for: Monotheism; many shared prophets (Abraham, Moses); holy books; Abraham as an ancestor of faith.

questions.a: Monotheism; many shared prophets (Abraham, Moses); holy books; Abraham as an ancestor of faith.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "What is the hijra?" Look for: Muhammad's 622 migration from Mecca to Medina.

questions.a: Muhammad's 622 migration from Mecca to Medina.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Arabian geography: deserts, oases, trade routes. 2) Mecca as trade and religious center. 3) Muhammad born c. 570 in Mecca. 4) Hijra 622. 5) Returned to Mecca 630, died 632. 6) Islam, Judaism and Christianity are monotheistic. Timeline: all dates correct with brief captions.

weeks.prep: Translated Qur'an excerpts on charity and justice (Fordham); Five Pillars organizer; images of the Dome of the Rock and the Great Mosque of Córdoba (Smarthistory).
misconceptions: Thinking all Muslims are Arab. Most Muslims today live outside the Arab world (e.g., Indonesia).
Confusing the Qur'an (believed by Muslims to be God's word revealed to Muhammad) with the Hadith (reports of Muhammad's sayings and actions).

days.guide: Read passages together. Your child summarizes each teaching in one sentence. Check before moving on: ask "What do the passages teach about charity?" Look for: Believers should give to the poor, orphans and travelers; wealth is a trust from God.

questions.q: What do the passages teach about charity?
questions.a: Believers should give to the poor, orphans and travelers; wealth is a trust from God.

days.guide: Your child makes a graphic organizer of the Five Pillars. Check before moving on: ask "Name the Five Pillars." Look for: Shahada (declaration of faith), Salat (prayer five times daily facing Mecca), Zakat (charity), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca once if able).

questions.a: Shahada (declaration of faith), Salat (prayer five times daily facing Mecca), Zakat (charity), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca once if able).

days.guide: Explain Sunnah and Sharia. Your child lists examples in daily life, commerce and family. Check before moving on: ask "What is the Sunnah?" Look for: The example of Muhammad's words and actions, recorded in the Hadith.

questions.a: The example of Muhammad's words and actions, recorded in the Hadith.
Honest weights and measures; rules against charging interest.

days.guide: Show images. Your child identifies minaret, mihrab, arabesque and calligraphy. Check before moving on: ask "What is a mihrab?" Look for: A niche in the wall showing the direction of Mecca (qibla) for prayer.

questions.a: A niche in the wall showing the direction of Mecca (qibla) for prayer.

questions.q: Why geometric and plant patterns rather than people?
questions.a: Islamic religious art generally avoids depicting people or animals in sacred spaces.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "What happens during Ramadan?" Look for: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset.

questions.a: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: Five Pillars named and described; Qur'an vs. Hadith; Sunnah; Sharia; mosque features (minaret, mihrab, dome, calligraphy); Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, Great Mosque in Córdoba.

weeks.prep: Map of Muslim expansion 632–750; Ibn Battuta excerpts (Fordham); description of Baghdad's round city.
misconceptions: Thinking Islam spread only by conquest. Trade, intermarriage and missionaries spread it in Africa and Southeast Asia.
Thinking Sunni and Shia split over beliefs about God. They split over who should lead after Muhammad.

days.guide: Your child maps the expansion of each caliphate. Check before moving on: ask "Capitals of the Umayyads and Abbasids?" Look for: Damascus; Baghdad.

questions.q: Capitals of the Umayyads and Abbasids?
questions.a: Damascus; Baghdad.

questions.q: How far did Umayyad rule reach?
questions.a: From Spain to the Indus River valley.

days.guide: Explain the succession dispute. Check before moving on: ask "Sunni view?" Look for: The community should choose the leader (they accepted Abu Bakr).

questions.a: The community should choose the leader (they accepted Abu Bakr).
Leadership belonged to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants.

days.guide: Read about Baghdad. Your child explains why it became a center. Check before moving on: ask "Why Baghdad?" Look for: Founded 762 on the Tigris near the Euphrates, on trade routes linking Asia, Africa and Europe; caliphs supported scholars.

questions.a: Founded 762 on the Tigris near the Euphrates, on trade routes linking Asia, Africa and Europe; caliphs supported scholars.

days.guide: Read Ibn Battuta excerpts. Your child traces his route. Check before moving on: ask "Who was Ibn Battuta?" Look for: A Moroccan Muslim scholar who traveled about 75,000 miles across Africa, the Middle East, India and China in the 1300s.

questions.a: A Moroccan Muslim scholar who traveled about 75,000 miles across Africa, the Middle East, India and China in the 1300s.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph on how trade spread Islam and Arabic. Check before moving on: ask "Evidence?" Look for: Merchants carried religion and Arabic along trade routes; Arabic became the language of trade, learning and religion.

questions.a: Merchants carried religion and Arabic along trade routes; Arabic became the language of trade, learning and religion.

weeks.assessment_key: Map: caliphates shaded with dates and capitals. Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence answering the prompt, at least two accurate specific facts or document references, explanation of how they support the claim, concluding sentence; 3 = accurate but thin explanation; 2 = general statements, few facts; 1 = off-topic or inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Paper plate, protractor, straw, string and washer for astrolabe; compass, ruler for geometric pattern; reading on the House of Wisdom.
misconceptions: Thinking Muslim scholars only preserved Greek knowledge. They added original work in algebra, medicine, optics and astronomy.
Thinking an astrolabe tells time only. It measures angles of stars to find latitude and time.

days.guide: Read about the House of Wisdom. Your child lists what scholars translated and why. Check before moving on: ask "What was the House of Wisdom?" Look for: A library and center in Baghdad where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic.

questions.q: What was the House of Wisdom?
questions.a: A library and center in Baghdad where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic.

days.guide: Show al-Khwarizmi's balancing method. Your child solves a simple equation and researches Ibn Sina. Check before moving on: ask "What word comes from al-Khwarizmi's book?" Look for: Algebra (from al-jabr); 'algorithm' comes from his name.

questions.q: What word comes from al-Khwarizmi's book?
questions.a: Algebra (from al-jabr); 'algorithm' comes from his name.
The Canon of Medicine, used in European universities for centuries.

days.guide: Build the astrolabe. At night, your child sights the North Star and reads the angle. Check before moving on: ask "What does the North Star's angle tell you?" Look for: Your latitude.

questions.q: What does the North Star's angle tell you?
questions.a: Your latitude.

days.guide: Model constructing an 8-point star with a compass. Your child draws a repeating pattern. Check before moving on: ask "Why geometric patterns?" Look for: They express infinite order and avoid images of living beings in religious spaces.

questions.a: They express infinite order and avoid images of living beings in religious spaces.

days.guide: Give the unit 2 test. Check before moving on: ask "Two Golden Age contributions?" Look for: Algebra; Ibn Sina's medical encyclopedia; improved astrolabes; optics (Ibn al-Haytham).

questions.a: Algebra; Ibn Sina's medical encyclopedia; improved astrolabes; optics (Ibn al-Haytham).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test: Arabia geography; Muhammad timeline; Five Pillars; Sunni-Shia; caliphates; Baghdad; Golden Age. Constructed response proficient: two contributions with scholar names and impact.

weeks.prep: Map of China; foam sheet, pencil and paint for stamp; invention chart.
misconceptions: Thinking the Silk Road was a single road. It was a network of routes.
Thinking China invented the printing press like Gutenberg's. China invented woodblock printing (and movable type) earlier.

days.guide: Show a map of China. Your child labels the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, the Grand Canal and Silk Road routes, then reads how the Sui (589) reunified China and the Tang expanded it. Ask why a canal linking north and south mattered.

questions.a: The Sui dynasty.
To connect the Yellow and Yangtze rivers for shipping grain north.

days.guide: Your child traces Buddhism's spread. Check before moving on: ask "Route?" Look for: India → Central Asia via Silk Road → China → Korea → Japan.

questions.a: India → Central Asia via Silk Road → China → Korea → Japan.

days.guide: Your child makes a chart of six inventions (paper, printing, compass, gunpowder, tea, porcelain) with columns for when, what it did, and how it changed the wider world. Check before moving on: ask "Global impact of the compass?" Look for: Enabled navigation and later the Age of Exploration.

questions.a: Enabled navigation and later the Age of Exploration.

days.guide: Your child draws a simple design, carves it into foam (reversing any letters), inks and prints several copies. Then read about the Diamond Sutra and discuss how woodblocks made copying faster. Check before moving on: ask "What is the Diamond Sutra?" Look for: The oldest dated printed book (868), a Buddhist text printed with woodblocks.

questions.a: The oldest dated printed book (868), a Buddhist text printed with woodblocks.

days.guide: Give the Tang and Song quiz without notes; review the invention chart together. Check before moving on: ask "Dates of the Tang and Song?" Look for: Tang 618–907; Song 960–1279.

questions.q: Dates of the Tang and Song?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: Sui reunification, Grand Canal, Tang and Song dates, Buddhism spread, inventions (paper, printing, compass, gunpowder, porcelain), Diamond Sutra 868.

weeks.prep: Analects excerpts; mock civil service exam (10 questions on the Analects).
misconceptions: Thinking Confucianism is mainly about gods. It focuses on ethics, relationships and good government.
Thinking the exams were open to everyone equally. Studying took years, so mostly wealthy families' sons passed.

days.guide: Read passages. Your child explains filial piety and the five relationships. Check before moving on: ask "The five relationships?" Look for: Ruler–subject, father–son, husband–wife, elder brother–younger brother, friend–friend.

questions.a: Ruler–subject, father–son, husband–wife, elder brother–younger brother, friend–friend.
Respect and obedience to parents and ancestors.

days.guide: Give a 10-question mock exam on the Analects under timed, silent conditions. Discuss: who could afford to prepare, and was the system fair? Check before moving on: ask "Why might exams be unfair?" Look for: Only those who could afford years of study could pass.

questions.a: Only those who could afford years of study could pass.

days.guide: Explain how passing exams created a class of scholar-officials. Your child compares this to modern civil service tests and job interviews. Check before moving on: ask "How were officials chosen?" Look for: By passing exams on Confucian classics — merit, not birth.

questions.a: By passing exams on Confucian classics — merit, not birth.

days.guide: Read a short passage about Zhu Xi. Your child lists which ideas came from Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism. Check before moving on: ask "What did Neo-Confucianism blend?" Look for: Confucian ethics with Buddhist and Daoist ideas about the universe and the mind.

questions.a: Confucian ethics with Buddhist and Daoist ideas about the universe and the mind.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph evaluating whether merit-based exams strengthened China, using two pieces of evidence and one counterargument. Check before moving on: ask "One argument for?" Look for: Educated, capable officials; stable government.

questions.a: Educated, capable officials; stable government.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence answering the prompt, at least two accurate specific facts or document references, explanation of how they support the claim, concluding sentence; 3 = accurate but thin explanation; 2 = general statements, few facts; 1 = off-topic or inaccurate. Proficient addresses both strengths (educated officials, stability) and weaknesses (favored wealthy, rigid focus on classics).

weeks.prep: Marco Polo excerpt on Kublai Khan's court; map of Zheng He's voyages; Mongol Empire map.
misconceptions: Thinking the Mongols only destroyed. The Pax Mongolica made trade safer across Eurasia.
Thinking Zheng He's voyages were to conquer. They displayed Ming power and gathered tribute.

days.guide: Your child maps the Mongol Empire and explains the Pax Mongolica. Check before moving on: ask "Who founded the empire?" Look for: Genghis Khan (1206).

questions.a: Genghis Khan (1206).
Period of relative peace under Mongol rule that made Silk Road trade safer.

days.guide: Read Marco Polo's description of Kublai Khan's court. Your child lists details and evaluates the source's reliability (who, when, purpose). Check before moving on: ask "Why question Polo?" Look for: He dictated it in prison years later, possibly exaggerating; some details are missing.

questions.a: He dictated it in prison years later, possibly exaggerating; some details are missing.

days.guide: Your child maps Zheng He's seven voyages and compares the size of his fleet and ships with Columbus's three ships in a chart. Check before moving on: ask "Dates?" Look for: 1405–1433.

questions.a: Zheng He's treasure ships were several times longer than Columbus's Santa María.

days.guide: Your child lists reasons the Ming ended the voyages and rebuilt the Great Wall, then debates you: was it a wise decision? Check before moving on: ask "Reasons?" Look for: Cost, Confucian disdain for trade, threats from the north requiring Great Wall rebuilding.

questions.a: Cost, Confucian disdain for trade, threats from the north requiring Great Wall rebuilding.

days.guide: Give the unit 3 test independently. Check before moving on: ask "Kublai Khan founded which dynasty?" Look for: Yuan dynasty.

questions.a: Yuan dynasty.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test: Sui/Tang/Song, Buddhism spread, inventions, Confucianism and exams, Mongols and Yuan, Marco Polo, Zheng He 1405–1433, Ming end voyages.

weeks.prep: West Africa vegetation-zone map, colored pencils; a bowl of salt and gold-painted rocks; al-Bakri's description of Ghana (1068, in Fordham or Levtzion & Hopkins).
misconceptions: Thinking Africa is all jungle or desert. West Africa has bands: Sahara desert, Sahel, savanna and forest.
Thinking salt was cheap everywhere. In the hot south it was scarce and needed to preserve food and replace salt lost by sweating.

days.guide: Your child colors the four zones and lists resources from each. Check before moving on: ask "Resource from the Sahara?" Look for: Salt (e.g., mines at Taghaza).

questions.a: Salt (e.g., mines at Taghaza).
Gold (Bambuk, Bure), kola nuts, ivory.

days.guide: Explain silent barter, then simulate it with your child. Check before moving on: ask "Why was salt worth gold?" Look for: People in the south needed salt to survive and preserve food but had none; northerners wanted gold.

questions.a: People in the south needed salt to survive and preserve food but had none; northerners wanted gold.
Traders left salt, withdrew; gold miners left gold beside it; trading continued until both were satisfied, without speaking.

days.guide: Read al-Bakri. Your child lists signs of wealth and power. Check before moving on: ask "Signs of the king's wealth?" Look for: Gold ornaments, horses with gold trappings, dogs with gold collars, and the king keeping all gold nuggets (people could trade gold dust).

questions.a: Gold ornaments, horses with gold trappings, dogs with gold collars, and the king keeping all gold nuggets (people could trade gold dust).

days.guide: Your child explains clans and crafts like blacksmithing. Check before moving on: ask "Why were blacksmiths important?" Look for: They made iron tools and weapons for farming and war, giving Ghana military strength.

questions.a: They made iron tools and weapons for farming and war, giving Ghana military strength.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "How did Ghana grow rich?" Look for: By taxing the gold-salt trade passing through its land.

questions.a: By taxing the gold-salt trade passing through its land.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: four vegetation zones; salt from the north, gold from the south; silent barter; Ghana taxed trade; king kept nuggets; capital Koumbi Saleh; iron weapons. Map: zones colored with resources.

weeks.prep: Retelling of the Epic of Sundiata; Catalan Atlas image (1375); readings on Timbuktu; Ibn Battuta's account of Mali.
misconceptions: Thinking Mansa Musa's gift-giving only helped Cairo. Flooding Cairo with gold lowered its value for years.
Thinking Timbuktu was a myth or tiny. It was a major center of Islamic scholarship with thousands of manuscripts.

days.guide: Read the epic retelling. Your child lists Sundiata's leadership qualities. Check before moving on: ask "What challenge did Sundiata overcome as a child?" Look for: He could not walk, but grew strong and became a great leader.

questions.q: What challenge did Sundiata overcome as a child?
questions.a: He could not walk, but grew strong and became a great leader.
Defeated Sumanguru at Kirina (c. 1235) and founded the Mali Empire.

days.guide: Show the Catalan Atlas. Your child explains what it shows and the effect of the hajj on Cairo. Check before moving on: ask "What does the atlas show?" Look for: Mansa Musa on a throne holding a gold nugget — Europeans saw Mali as fabulously rich.

questions.a: Mansa Musa on a throne holding a gold nugget — Europeans saw Mali as fabulously rich.
He gave away so much gold in 1324 that its value fell in Cairo for years.

days.guide: Your child researches Timbuktu. Check before moving on: ask "What made Timbuktu famous?" Look for: Sankore and Djinguereber mosques, scholars and manuscripts on law, science and religion.

questions.a: Sankore and Djinguereber mosques, scholars and manuscripts on law, science and religion.

days.guide: Read Ibn Battuta's account. Your child lists admired and criticized things. Check before moving on: ask "Admired?" Look for: Safety on roads, justice, devotion to prayer.

questions.a: Safety on roads, justice, devotion to prayer.
Some customs, like women servants' dress and the ruler's small gift to him.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph on how trade spread Islam and Arabic. Check before moving on: ask "Example evidence?" Look for: Muslim merchants traveled trans-Saharan routes; rulers like Mansa Musa adopted Islam; Arabic became the language of scholarship in Timbuktu.

questions.a: Muslim merchants traveled trans-Saharan routes; rulers like Mansa Musa adopted Islam; Arabic became the language of scholarship in Timbuktu.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence answering the prompt, at least two accurate specific facts or document references, explanation of how they support the claim, concluding sentence; 3 = accurate but thin explanation; 2 = general statements, few facts; 1 = off-topic or inaccurate. Source analysis: identifies the author's perspective (Ibn Battuta as an outside Muslim scholar).

weeks.prep: Recorded griot performance with kora (search 'griot kora'); 8 West African proverbs; interview questions for a relative.
misconceptions: Thinking oral history is unreliable compared with written history. Griots trained for years to memorize and preserve accurate histories and genealogies.
Thinking proverbs are just sayings. They pass on values and wisdom.

days.guide: Listen to a griot. Your child explains the griot's role. Check before moving on: ask "What is a griot?" Look for: A West African storyteller, historian and musician who preserves family histories, genealogies and events orally.

questions.a: A West African storyteller, historian and musician who preserves family histories, genealogies and events orally.
A 21-string harp-lute.

days.guide: Your child interprets 8 proverbs and writes two family proverbs. Check before moving on: ask "Interpret: 'Rain does not fall on one roof alone.'" Look for: Troubles come to everyone; we share hardships.

questions.q: Interpret: 'Rain does not fall on one roof alone.'
questions.a: Troubles come to everyone; we share hardships.

days.guide: Your child interviews a relative and retells it as a griot would. Check before moving on: ask "What makes it griot-like?" Look for: Spoken aloud from memory, with names, ancestors and a lesson.

questions.a: Spoken aloud from memory, with names, ancestors and a lesson.

days.guide: Read about Songhai's rise. Check before moving on: ask "Who expanded Songhai?" Look for: Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad.

questions.a: Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad.
1591, to a Moroccan army with guns.

days.guide: Give the unit 4 test; your child performs the oral story. Check before moving on: ask "Three West African empires in order?" Look for: Ghana, Mali, Songhai.

questions.q: Three West African empires in order?
questions.a: Ghana, Mali, Songhai.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test: vegetation zones, gold-salt trade, Ghana, Sundiata, Mansa Musa 1324, Timbuktu, Ibn Battuta, griots, Songhai. Oral history rubric: memorized, includes names and events, clear lesson, expressive delivery.

weeks.prep: Map of Japan; Seventeen-Article Constitution excerpt (604); excerpt from The Tale of Genji or The Pillow Book; shoebox, sand, rocks, fork for rock garden.
misconceptions: Thinking Japan copied China completely. It borrowed selectively (writing, Buddhism, Confucianism) and adapted.
Thinking Zen and Pure Land are the same. Pure Land emphasizes faith in Amida Buddha; Zen emphasizes meditation.

days.guide: Your child maps Japan's four main islands, mountains and distance to Korea and China. Check before moving on: ask "Four main islands?" Look for: Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, Shikoku.

questions.a: Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, Shikoku.
Mountains cover most land, so people lived on coastal plains; the sea gave food and some protection.

days.guide: Read the constitution. Your child marks Confucian and Buddhist ideas. Check before moving on: ask "Example of Confucian idea?" Look for: Harmony; obeying superiors; officials act with propriety.

questions.a: Harmony; obeying superiors; officials act with propriety.
Revere the three treasures: Buddha, the Law, the monks.

days.guide: Read the excerpt. Your child describes Heian court life. Check before moving on: ask "Who wrote The Tale of Genji?" Look for: Murasaki Shikibu, a court lady, around 1000.

questions.q: Who wrote The Tale of Genji?
questions.a: Murasaki Shikibu, a court lady, around 1000.
Beauty, poetry, elegant dress and manners.

days.guide: Compare Pure Land and Zen; build a rock garden. Check before moving on: ask "Why did Zen appeal to samurai?" Look for: Its discipline and meditation built focus and self-control.

questions.q: Why did Zen appeal to samurai?
questions.a: Its discipline and meditation built focus and self-control.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Prince Shotoku's goals?" Look for: Strengthen central government and spread Buddhism.

questions.a: Strengthen central government and spread Buddhism.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: islands, Shotoku and Chinese influence, Heian period (794–1185), Murasaki Shikibu, Pure Land vs Zen. Source analysis: identifies Confucian and Buddhist ideas with quotes.

weeks.prep: Excerpts on Bushido; comparison chart (Japanese vs European feudalism); research materials on Noh, haiku or tea ceremony.
misconceptions: Thinking the emperor held real power under the shogun. The emperor was mostly a figurehead.
Thinking Bushido was written down from the start. Many ideas were codified later (Edo period).

days.guide: Explain the Gempei War and Minamoto Yoritomo. Your child summarizes. Check before moving on: ask "Who became the first shogun of the Kamakura shogunate?" Look for: Minamoto Yoritomo, 1192.

questions.q: Who became the first shogun of the Kamakura shogunate?
questions.a: Minamoto Yoritomo, 1192.

days.guide: Your child draws the feudal pyramid. Check before moving on: ask "Order?" Look for: Emperor (figurehead), shogun, daimyo, samurai, peasants, artisans, merchants.

questions.a: Emperor (figurehead), shogun, daimyo, samurai, peasants, artisans, merchants.

days.guide: Read excerpts. Your child explains values. Check before moving on: ask "Bushido values?" Look for: Loyalty to one's lord, honor, courage, self-discipline.

questions.a: Loyalty to one's lord, honor, courage, self-discipline.

days.guide: Your child researches and presents a cultural legacy. Check before moving on: ask "Haiku pattern?" Look for: Three lines of 5-7-5 syllables, often about nature.

questions.a: Three lines of 5-7-5 syllables, often about nature.
Matsuo Basho.

days.guide: Give the unit 5 test. Check before moving on: ask "How was Japanese feudalism like European?" Look for: Land and protection exchanged for loyalty and military service.

questions.q: How was Japanese feudalism like European?
questions.a: Land and protection exchanged for loyalty and military service.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test: geography, Shotoku, Heian culture, Buddhism types, Kamakura shogunate 1192, feudal pyramid, Bushido, cultural legacies, comparison with Europe.

weeks.prep: Physical map of Europe; Rule of St. Benedict excerpt; Book of Kells images; gold marker; Einhard's Life of Charlemagne excerpt.
misconceptions: Thinking the Middle Ages were 'dark' with no learning. Monasteries preserved books and learning.
Thinking Charlemagne was French or German only. His empire covered much of both.

days.guide: Your child labels a physical map of Europe: Rhine, Danube, Alps, Pyrenees, North European Plain, Mediterranean, North and Baltic seas, then explains how each affected trade and settlement. Check before moving on: ask "How did rivers help?" Look for: Rhine and Danube were trade routes.

questions.a: Rhine and Danube were trade routes.
Alps and Pyrenees.

days.guide: Read the Rule. Your child describes monastery life. Check before moving on: ask "Daily life?" Look for: Prayer at set hours, manual work, reading, obedience — 'pray and work'.

questions.a: Prayer at set hours, manual work, reading, obedience — 'pray and work'.

days.guide: Show Book of Kells images. Your child designs an illuminated first letter of their name with interlace patterns and gold marker. Check before moving on: ask "What is an illuminated manuscript?" Look for: Handwritten book decorated with gold, color and designs.

questions.a: Handwritten book decorated with gold, color and designs.

days.guide: Read Einhard. Your child lists achievements. Check before moving on: ask "When was Charlemagne crowned emperor?" Look for: 800 CE by Pope Leo III.

questions.a: 800 CE by Pope Leo III.
Unified much of western Europe, promoted learning and schools, spread Christianity.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Why were monasteries important?" Look for: Preserved learning, copied books, helped the poor.

questions.a: Preserved learning, copied books, helped the poor.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: rivers, mountains, plains; Benedict's Rule; monks copied manuscripts; Charlemagne crowned 800; Carolingian Renaissance.

weeks.prep: Manor diagram; oath of fealty (Fordham); guild charter template.
misconceptions: Thinking serfs were slaves. Serfs were bound to the land but could not be sold separately.
Thinking knights owned land outright. They held fiefs in exchange for service.

days.guide: Draw the feudal pyramid together (king, lords, knights, peasants/serfs). Your child explains the exchange of land for loyalty and service. Check before moving on: ask "What did vassals receive and give?" Look for: Received land (fief) and protection; gave loyalty and military service.

questions.q: What did vassals receive and give?
questions.a: Received land (fief) and protection; gave loyalty and military service.

days.guide: Read an oath of fealty aloud. Role-play a homage ceremony with your child as vassal; then discuss what each side promised. Check before moving on: ask "What does homage involve?" Look for: Vassal kneels, places hands between lord's, swears loyalty.

questions.a: Vassal kneels, places hands between lord's, swears loyalty.

days.guide: Your child labels a manor diagram (manor house, church, fields, mill, village, commons) and calculates the gain from three-field rotation compared with two-field. Check before moving on: ask "How much more land was planted?" Look for: From one-half to two-thirds — a one-third increase in planted area.

questions.q: How much more land was planted?
questions.a: From one-half to two-thirds — a one-third increase in planted area.

days.guide: Read about guilds. Your child designs a guild charter for a craft with rules for apprentices, journeymen, masters, prices and quality. Check before moving on: ask "Guild stages?" Look for: Apprentice, journeyman, master.

questions.a: Apprentice, journeyman, master.

days.guide: Your child writes a diary entry of a serf, knight or apprentice with at least five accurate historical details. Check before moving on: ask "Accurate serf details?" Look for: Work lord's fields several days a week, pay fees, live in a one-room hut.

questions.a: Work lord's fields several days a week, pay fees, live in a one-room hut.

weeks.assessment_key: Diary rubric: 4 = accurate role details, at least five historical facts, first-person voice, vivid; 3 = some details; 2 = generic; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Magna Carta translation (British Library); U.S. Bill of Rights.
misconceptions: Thinking Magna Carta created democracy immediately. It mainly protected barons at first.
Thinking habeas corpus came directly in 1215. It developed later (1679 Act).

days.guide: Read about Canossa. Your child explains investiture. Check before moving on: ask "What was the investiture controversy?" Look for: Conflict over who appointed bishops — pope or king.

questions.a: Conflict over who appointed bishops — pope or king.
Henry IV stood in the snow seeking the pope's forgiveness.

days.guide: Read clauses 39 and 40. Your child restates them. Check before moving on: ask "Clause 39 in modern words?" Look for: No free man can be arrested or punished except by lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land.

questions.a: No free man can be arrested or punished except by lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land.
Justice won't be sold, denied or delayed.

days.guide: Your child traces a timeline from Magna Carta (1215) to the Model Parliament (1295) to the Habeas Corpus Act (1679), explaining each step. Check before moving on: ask "Model Parliament?" Look for: 1295, Edward I.

questions.a: 1295, Edward I.

days.guide: Your child makes a chart connecting Magna Carta clauses to U.S. Bill of Rights amendments. Check before moving on: ask "Clause 39 connects to?" Look for: 5th Amendment due process, 6th Amendment jury trial.

questions.a: 5th Amendment due process, 6th Amendment jury trial.

days.guide: Give the semester 1 checkpoint covering units 1–6. Check before moving on: ask "When was Magna Carta signed?" Look for: 1215, King John at Runnymede.

questions.a: 1215, King John at Runnymede.

weeks.assessment_key: Magna Carta chart: clause, modern meaning, Bill of Rights connection. Semester checkpoint key: Rome/Byzantium, Islam, China, West Africa, Japan, Europe facts as in prior quizzes.

weeks.prep: Accounts of Urban II's speech at Clermont (Fordham has several versions); Ibn al-Athir excerpt on the 1099 capture of Jerusalem; map of Iberia for the Reconquista. Preview: sources describe massacres.
misconceptions: Thinking the Crusades were only about religion. Motives included land, wealth, adventure and political power.
Thinking Muslims, Christians and Jews never lived peacefully together. In al-Andalus (Córdoba), there were long periods of coexistence (convivencia).

days.guide: Read two versions of Urban's speech. Your child lists his reasons. Check before moving on: ask "Urban's reasons?" Look for: Help the Byzantine emperor against the Seljuk Turks, retake Jerusalem, promise forgiveness of sins, and redirect knights from fighting each other.

questions.a: Help the Byzantine emperor against the Seljuk Turks, retake Jerusalem, promise forgiveness of sins, and redirect knights from fighting each other.
1095, Clermont, France.

days.guide: Compare a Christian and Muslim account of 1099. Check before moving on: ask "How do the perspectives differ?" Look for: Christian chroniclers celebrate it as God's victory; Ibn al-Athir describes it as a slaughter of Muslims and a disaster.

questions.a: Christian chroniclers celebrate it as God's victory; Ibn al-Athir describes it as a slaughter of Muslims and a disaster.

days.guide: Your child charts effects on each group and trade. Check before moving on: ask "Effect on Jews?" Look for: Crusaders massacred Jewish communities in the Rhineland (1096).

questions.a: Crusaders massacred Jewish communities in the Rhineland (1096).
Increased European demand for Eastern goods, enriching Italian cities like Venice.

days.guide: Read about convivencia; map the Reconquista. Check before moving on: ask "When did the Reconquista end?" Look for: 1492, with the fall of Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella.

questions.a: 1492, with the fall of Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella.

questions.q: What happened to Spain's Jews that year?
questions.a: They were expelled unless they converted.

days.guide: Your child writes a perspective paragraph. Check before moving on: ask "What should it compare?" Look for: Each author's background, purpose and how it shapes the account.

questions.a: Each author's background, purpose and how it shapes the account.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence answering the prompt, at least two accurate specific facts or document references, explanation of how they support the claim, concluding sentence; 3 = accurate but thin explanation; 2 = general statements, few facts; 1 = off-topic or inaccurate. Proficient names both authors, their perspectives, and quotes or details from each.

weeks.prep: Plague spread map; Boccaccio's Decameron introduction excerpt; population data; images of Gothic cathedrals. Preview: Boccaccio describes death vividly.
misconceptions: Thinking people knew germs caused the plague. They blamed bad air, God's punishment, or scapegoated Jews.
Thinking the plague had only negative effects. Labor shortages raised wages and weakened serfdom.

days.guide: Your child maps the plague's spread from Central Asia to Caffa to Sicily (1347) across Europe. Check before moving on: ask "How did it spread?" Look for: Along trade routes by fleas on rats and through people.

questions.a: Along trade routes by fleas on rats and through people.
About one-third to one-half.

days.guide: Read Boccaccio. Your child lists social effects. Check before moving on: ask "Effects?" Look for: People abandoned sick family members, mass graves, some fled or partied, others isolated themselves.

questions.a: People abandoned sick family members, mass graves, some fled or partied, others isolated themselves.

days.guide: Your child explains how the plague weakened feudalism. Check before moving on: ask "Why?" Look for: Fewer workers meant peasants could demand higher wages or leave manors.

questions.a: Fewer workers meant peasants could demand higher wages or leave manors.

days.guide: Read about Aquinas and Gothic cathedrals. Check before moving on: ask "Aquinas's goal?" Look for: Show faith and reason (Aristotle) work together.

questions.a: Show faith and reason (Aristotle) work together.
Pointed arches, flying buttresses, stained glass.

days.guide: Give the unit 6 test. Check before moving on: ask "Effect of Magna Carta?" Look for: Limited the king's power.

questions.a: Limited the king's power.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test: geography, monasteries, Charlemagne, feudalism, manors, guilds, investiture, Magna Carta, Crusades, Reconquista, Black Death, Aquinas, Gothic architecture.

weeks.prep: Map of Mesoamerica; Maya number chart; Tzolk'in calendar converter (online).
misconceptions: Thinking the Maya disappeared. Millions of Maya people live today.
Thinking Maya numbers are base 10. They are base 20 and include zero.

days.guide: Your child maps the Yucatán, highlands and lowland rainforest and explains slash-and-burn farming and terraces. Check before moving on: ask "Farming methods?" Look for: Slash-and-burn (milpa), terraces, raised fields.

questions.a: Slash-and-burn (milpa), terraces, raised fields.

days.guide: View images of Tikal and Chichén Itzá. Your child describes pyramids, ball courts and plazas and what they suggest about Maya life. Check before moving on: ask "Purpose of ball courts?" Look for: Ritual ball games with religious meaning.

questions.a: Ritual ball games with religious meaning.

days.guide: Teach dots (1), bars (5), shell (0). Your child writes 1–100. Check before moving on: ask "Write 17." Look for: Three bars and two dots.

questions.a: Three bars and two dots.
One dot in the twenties place over a shell in the ones place.

days.guide: Your child uses an online converter to find their birthday in the Tzolk'in and writes their name using syllable glyphs. Check before moving on: ask "How many days in the Tzolk'in?" Look for: 260.

questions.q: How many days in the Tzolk'in?

days.guide: Give the Maya quiz without notes. Check before moving on: ask "Maya Classic period?" Look for: About 250–900 CE.

questions.a: About 250–900 CE.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: geography, farming, city-states, base 20 with zero, 260-day Tzolk'in and 365-day Haab', glyph writing. Math: 1–100 correct.

weeks.prep: Map of Tenochtitlan; Codex Mendoza images; string for quipu.
misconceptions: Thinking the Aztec called themselves Aztec. They called themselves Mexica.
Thinking the Inca had writing. They used quipus to record numbers.

days.guide: Your child studies Tenochtitlan and chinampas. Check before moving on: ask "What were chinampas?" Look for: Artificial island farms built in the lake.

questions.a: Artificial island farms built in the lake.
1325 on Lake Texcoco.

days.guide: Analyze Codex Mendoza tribute pages. Check before moving on: ask "What was tribute?" Look for: Goods conquered peoples had to pay the Aztec.

questions.a: Goods conquered peoples had to pay the Aztec.

days.guide: Map the Inca road; make a quipu. Check before moving on: ask "How long was the road?" Look for: About 25,000 miles (40,000 km).

questions.a: About 25,000 miles (40,000 km).
Relay runners carrying messages.

days.guide: Your child completes a comparison chart of Maya, Aztec and Inca government, economy, religion and achievements. Check before moving on: ask "Inca capital?" Look for: Cusco.

questions.a: Cusco.

days.guide: Give the Aztec and Inca quiz without notes. Check before moving on: ask "Inca labor tax?" Look for: Mit'a.

questions.a: Mit'a.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: Tenochtitlan, chinampas, tribute, Aztec classes, Inca roads, quipu, mit'a, Cusco. Chart: government, economy, religion, achievements for all three.

weeks.prep: Excerpt of Cortés's second letter; Broken Spears excerpt; 6 documents for DBQ.
misconceptions: Thinking a few hundred Spaniards defeated the Aztec alone. Thousands of Indigenous allies (Tlaxcalans) joined.
Thinking guns were the main factor. Disease and allies mattered more.

days.guide: Read Cortés's letter. Check before moving on: ask "How does Cortés describe Tenochtitlan?" Look for: As a magnificent city with a huge market, compared to Spanish cities.

questions.a: As a magnificent city with a huge market, compared to Spanish cities.

days.guide: Read the Aztec account; compare. Check before moving on: ask "Aztec perspective?" Look for: Grief, devastation, Spanish greed for gold.

questions.a: Grief, devastation, Spanish greed for gold.

days.guide: Explain Pizarro's victory. Check before moving on: ask "Factors?" Look for: Inca civil war (Atahualpa vs Huáscar), smallpox, steel weapons, horses, capturing Atahualpa at Cajamarca 1532.

questions.a: Inca civil war (Atahualpa vs Huáscar), smallpox, steel weapons, horses, capturing Atahualpa at Cajamarca 1532.

days.guide: Your child analyzes 6 documents, noting each one's author, date and the cause it supports, then groups them into categories. Check before moving on: ask "Common causes?" Look for: Disease, allies, technology, internal divisions.

questions.a: Disease, allies, technology, internal divisions.

days.guide: Your child writes the DBQ essay, then takes the short unit 7 test. Check before moving on: ask "When did Tenochtitlan fall?" Look for: 1521.

weeks.assessment_key: DBQ rubric: thesis with 3 causes, evidence from 4+ documents, explanation, sourcing. Unit 7 test: Maya, Aztec, Inca, conquest.

weeks.prep: Map of Italian city-states; Petrarch letter and Pico excerpt.
misconceptions: Thinking the Renaissance rejected religion. Most humanists were Christian.
Thinking the Renaissance started everywhere at once. It began in Italy.

days.guide: Your child maps city-states and explains why Italy. Check before moving on: ask "Why Italy?" Look for: Trade wealth, Roman ruins, contact with Byzantine and Muslim scholars.

questions.a: Trade wealth, Roman ruins, contact with Byzantine and Muslim scholars.

days.guide: Read Petrarch's letter to Cicero and the Pico excerpt aloud. Your child writes a definition of humanism with one quote from each. Check before moving on: ask "Humanism?" Look for: Study of classical texts and focus on human potential.

questions.a: Study of classical texts and focus on human potential.

days.guide: Your child researches the Medici as bankers and patrons and lists three works they funded. Check before moving on: ask "How did the Medici get rich?" Look for: Banking.

questions.q: How did the Medici get rich?
questions.a: Banking.
Donatello, Botticelli, Michelangelo.

days.guide: Your child explains how Venice's location and trade routes made it rich. Check before moving on: ask "Venice's advantage?" Look for: Location on the Adriatic, trade with Byzantium and Muslim lands.

questions.a: Location on the Adriatic, trade with Byzantium and Muslim lands.

days.guide: Give the Renaissance origins quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Father of humanism?" Look for: Petrarch.

questions.a: Petrarch.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: why Italy, humanism, Petrarch, Medici, Venice, Florence.

weeks.prep: Smarthistory images; ruler, sketchbook; Dante or Machiavelli excerpt.
misconceptions: Thinking perspective existed before the Renaissance. Linear perspective was developed by Brunelleschi.
Thinking Machiavelli advocated evil. He described how rulers keep power.

days.guide: Demonstrate a horizon line and one vanishing point. Your child draws a hallway or street with lines converging to the point. Check before moving on: ask "What is a vanishing point?" Look for: The point where parallel lines appear to meet.

questions.a: The point where parallel lines appear to meet.

days.guide: Show Leonardo's notebook pages. Your child designs an invention page with mirror-writing labels and sketches. Check before moving on: ask "Leonardo's interests?" Look for: Anatomy, flight, engineering, painting.

questions.a: Anatomy, flight, engineering, painting.

days.guide: Show the Sistine Chapel ceiling and The School of Athens. Your child identifies classical and humanist themes in each. Check before moving on: ask "Who is at the center of The School of Athens?" Look for: Plato and Aristotle.

questions.q: Who is at the center of The School of Athens?
questions.a: Plato and Aristotle.

days.guide: Read an excerpt from Dante's Inferno or The Prince together. Discuss its main ideas and whether they still apply. Check before moving on: ask "Machiavelli's famous idea?" Look for: It is safer for a ruler to be feared than loved if he cannot be both.

questions.a: It is safer for a ruler to be feared than loved if he cannot be both.

days.guide: Your child writes a museum card (title, artist, date, medium, significance) for one artwork. Check before moving on: ask "Museum card includes?" Look for: Title, artist, date, significance.

questions.a: Title, artist, date, significance.

weeks.assessment_key: Perspective drawing: one vanishing point, converging lines. Museum card: accurate facts and significance.

weeks.prep: Letter stamps or potato-carved letters, ink pad, paper; map of European printing presses by 1500; images of Dürer and van Eyck works.
misconceptions: Thinking Gutenberg invented printing. He invented a movable-metal-type press in Europe (c. 1450); China had woodblock printing and movable type centuries earlier.
Thinking literacy rose overnight. It grew gradually as books became cheaper.

days.guide: Read about Gutenberg. Your child compares copying by hand vs printing. Check before moving on: ask "When was the Gutenberg Bible printed?" Look for: About 1455.

questions.q: When was the Gutenberg Bible printed?
questions.a: About 1455.

questions.q: Effect on book cost and time?
questions.a: A scribe took months or more per book; presses produced many copies quickly and cheaply.

days.guide: Your child sets type with letter stamps (reversed!) and prints a message. Check before moving on: ask "Why must type be reversed?" Look for: It prints as a mirror image.

questions.a: It prints as a mirror image.

days.guide: Your child maps presses and explains effects. Check before moving on: ask "Effects?" Look for: More books, higher literacy, books in vernacular languages, faster spread of ideas.

questions.a: More books, higher literacy, books in vernacular languages, faster spread of ideas.

days.guide: Compare northern and Italian artists. Check before moving on: ask "Van Eyck's contribution?" Look for: Oil painting with fine detail (Arnolfini Portrait).

questions.a: Oil painting with fine detail (Arnolfini Portrait).
Woodcuts and engravings, self-portraits.

days.guide: Your child writes a cause-effect paragraph. Check before moving on: ask "Strong cause-effect chain?" Look for: Press → cheaper books → more readers → ideas (like Luther's) spread fast.

questions.a: Press → cheaper books → more readers → ideas (like Luther's) spread fast.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence answering the prompt, at least two accurate specific facts or document references, explanation of how they support the claim, concluding sentence; 3 = accurate but thin explanation; 2 = general statements, few facts; 1 = off-topic or inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Excerpts of the 95 Theses; account of the Diet of Worms; Reformation pamphlet images.
misconceptions: Thinking Luther wanted to start a new church. He first wanted to reform the Catholic Church.
Thinking indulgences were 'permission to sin.' They were believed to reduce punishment for sins already forgiven; abuses arose when they were sold.

days.guide: Your child charts causes of discontent. Check before moving on: ask "Causes?" Look for: Western Schism (1378–1417) with rival popes, wealthy and corrupt clergy, sale of indulgences.

questions.a: Western Schism (1378–1417) with rival popes, wealthy and corrupt clergy, sale of indulgences.

days.guide: Read 10 theses; restate. Check before moving on: ask "Thesis 86 restated?" Look for: Why doesn't the rich pope build St. Peter's Basilica with his own money instead of poor people's?

questions.a: Why doesn't the rich pope build St. Peter's Basilica with his own money instead of poor people's?
1517, Wittenberg.

days.guide: Read Luther at Worms. Check before moving on: ask "Why did Luther refuse to recant?" Look for: His conscience was bound by Scripture; he would recant only if proven wrong by Scripture and reason.

questions.q: Why did Luther refuse to recant?
questions.a: His conscience was bound by Scripture; he would recant only if proven wrong by Scripture and reason.

days.guide: Explain printing and Reformation. Check before moving on: ask "How did printing help Luther?" Look for: Pamphlets and his German Bible spread his ideas quickly to many people.

questions.a: Pamphlets and his German Bible spread his ideas quickly to many people.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Diet of Worms year?" Look for: 1521.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: causes of discontent, indulgences, Tetzel, 95 Theses 1517, Diet of Worms 1521, printing press role, Luther's key beliefs (faith alone, Bible authority).

weeks.prep: Religious map of Europe c. 1600; four-column reformer chart.
misconceptions: Thinking all Protestants agreed. Lutherans, Calvinists and Anglicans differed.
Thinking Henry VIII changed doctrines a lot. He mainly changed who led the church.

days.guide: Your child compares four reformers. Check before moving on: ask "Erasmus?" Look for: Criticized corruption but stayed Catholic.

questions.a: Criticized corruption but stayed Catholic.
Predestination; led Geneva.

days.guide: Explain Henry VIII. Check before moving on: ask "Why did Henry break with Rome?" Look for: The pope wouldn't annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon; Act of Supremacy (1534) made him head of the Church of England.

questions.q: Why did Henry break with Rome?
questions.a: The pope wouldn't annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon; Act of Supremacy (1534) made him head of the Church of England.

days.guide: Explain congregational self-government. Check before moving on: ask "How did it influence democracy?" Look for: Members elected leaders and governed themselves, practicing self-rule.

questions.a: Members elected leaders and governed themselves, practicing self-rule.

days.guide: Color the map; predict colonization effects. Check before moving on: ask "Catholic regions c. 1600?" Look for: Spain, Portugal, Italy, France (mostly), southern Germany.

questions.a: Spain, Portugal, Italy, France (mostly), southern Germany.
England, Scotland, Scandinavia, northern Germany, Netherlands.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph. Check before moving on: ask "Key idea?" Look for: Questioning church authority encouraged questioning political authority.

questions.a: Questioning church authority encouraged questioning political authority.

weeks.assessment_key: Map: correct shading and legend. Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence answering the prompt, at least two accurate specific facts or document references, explanation of how they support the claim, concluding sentence; 3 = accurate but thin explanation; 2 = general statements, few facts; 1 = off-topic or inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Council of Trent summaries; Calisphere images of California missions; timeline sorting cards. Preview: missions discussion includes harm to Native Californians.
misconceptions: Thinking the Counter-Reformation only fought Protestants. It also reformed abuses inside the Catholic Church.
Thinking Jesuits founded California's missions. Franciscans (Junípero Serra) founded the 21 Alta California missions (1769–1823).

days.guide: Your child charts changes and continuities from Trent. Check before moving on: ask "What changed?" Look for: Ended sale of indulgences abuses, required training for priests (seminaries).

questions.a: Ended sale of indulgences abuses, required training for priests (seminaries).
Seven sacraments, authority of pope and tradition.

days.guide: Research Loyola and Jesuits. Check before moving on: ask "Founded?" Look for: 1540, Ignatius of Loyola.

questions.a: 1540, Ignatius of Loyola.
Francis Xavier in Asia.

days.guide: Analyze mission images. Check before moving on: ask "Impacts on Native Californians?" Look for: Forced labor, loss of culture and land, deadly diseases; population declined sharply.

questions.a: Forced labor, loss of culture and land, deadly diseases; population declined sharply.

days.guide: Play the timeline sorting game. Check before moving on: ask "Order: Gutenberg Bible, 95 Theses, Council of Trent begins." Look for: 1455, 1517, 1545.

questions.q: Order: Gutenberg Bible, 95 Theses, Council of Trent begins.

days.guide: Give the unit 8 test. Check before moving on: ask "Who was Ignatius of Loyola?" Look for: Founder of the Jesuits.

questions.a: Founder of the Jesuits.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test: Renaissance origins, humanism, art, printing, Reformation causes, Luther, other reformers, Henry VIII, Council of Trent, Jesuits.

weeks.prep: Flashlight or lamp, balls; Galileo's Starry Messenger excerpt; objects of different masses.
misconceptions: Thinking heavier objects fall faster. Without air resistance, they fall at the same rate.
Thinking the Church opposed all science. It supported much astronomy but objected to Galileo's challenge.

days.guide: Your child makes a chain showing Greek, Muslim and Renaissance contributions leading to the Scientific Revolution. Check before moving on: ask "Contributions?" Look for: Greek observation, Muslim scholars (Ibn al-Haytham's optics), Renaissance questioning.

questions.a: Greek observation, Muslim scholars (Ibn al-Haytham's optics), Renaissance questioning.

days.guide: Model geocentric and heliocentric systems. Check before moving on: ask "Who proposed heliocentric model?" Look for: Copernicus (1543).

questions.a: Copernicus (1543).
Planets move in elliptical orbits.

days.guide: Read Galileo's observations. Check before moving on: ask "What did Galileo see?" Look for: Four moons orbiting Jupiter, mountains on the Moon.

questions.a: Four moons orbiting Jupiter, mountains on the Moon.
Tried in 1633, forced to recant, house arrest.

days.guide: Drop objects of different masses from the same height together. Your child observes and explains Newton's law of universal gravitation. Check before moving on: ask "Newton's law of universal gravitation?" Look for: Every mass attracts every other mass.

questions.a: Every mass attracts every other mass.

days.guide: Give the Scientific Revolution quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Newton's major work?" Look for: Principia (1687).

questions.a: Principia (1687).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: geocentric vs heliocentric, Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, Newton, roots.

weeks.prep: Jar, balloon, rubber band, straw (barometer); magnifier.
misconceptions: Thinking empiricism and rationalism are opposite enemies.
Thinking science and religion always conflicted.

days.guide: Read short quotes from Bacon and Descartes. Your child compares empiricism and rationalism in a T-chart. Check before moving on: ask "Bacon?" Look for: Knowledge through observation and experiment (empiricism).

questions.a: Knowledge through observation and experiment (empiricism).
'I think, therefore I am'; reason (rationalism).

days.guide: Stretch a balloon over a jar, tape a straw pointer, and mark a scale. Your child records readings daily for a week. Check before moving on: ask "Rising pointer means?" Look for: Higher air pressure, usually fair weather.

questions.a: Higher air pressure, usually fair weather.

days.guide: Read about Leeuwenhoek and Hooke. Your child draws magnified objects (salt, a leaf, fabric) with a magnifier. Check before moving on: ask "Hooke's discovery?" Look for: Named 'cells' after seeing cork.

questions.a: Named 'cells' after seeing cork.
Saw microorganisms.

days.guide: Discuss examples of scientists with religious beliefs (Kepler, Newton) and how science and religion coexisted. Check before moving on: ask "Example?" Look for: Newton and Kepler were devout Christians.

questions.a: Newton and Kepler were devout Christians.

days.guide: Your child writes how scientific rationalism encouraged questioning political authority, with an example. Check before moving on: ask "Key idea?" Look for: If nature follows laws discovered by reason, maybe government should too.

questions.a: If nature follows laws discovered by reason, maybe government should too.

weeks.assessment_key: Written explanation rubric: links scientific method to questioning tradition, gives example (Enlightenment thinkers), accurate.

weeks.prep: World map; Columbus's journal excerpt (Oct 1492); Library of Congress maps from 1450 and 1570.
misconceptions: Thinking Columbus proved the Earth was round. Educated Europeans already knew.
Thinking Columbus 'discovered' empty land. Millions of people lived there.

days.guide: Your child lists motives for exploration (God, gold, glory) and the technologies that made it possible. Check before moving on: ask "God, gold and glory?" Look for: Spread Christianity, gain wealth, win fame.

questions.a: Spread Christianity, gain wealth, win fame.
Caravel, astrolabe, magnetic compass, better maps.

days.guide: Your child maps the voyages of Dias, da Gama, Columbus, Magellan and Cabrillo with dates. Check before moving on: ask "Dias?" Look for: Rounded Cape of Good Hope 1488.

questions.a: Rounded Cape of Good Hope 1488.
Explored California coast 1542.

days.guide: Read Columbus's October 1492 journal entry. Your child analyzes his descriptions of the Taíno and what they reveal about his intentions. Check before moving on: ask "How does he describe the Taíno?" Look for: As gentle and generous, but thinks they'd make good servants and easily be converted.

questions.q: How does he describe the Taíno?
questions.a: As gentle and generous, but thinks they'd make good servants and easily be converted.

days.guide: Compare maps from 1450 and 1570. Your child lists what changed and how it reflects a new worldview. Check before moving on: ask "Change?" Look for: Americas appear; Europeans realized a new continent existed.

questions.a: Americas appear; Europeans realized a new continent existed.

days.guide: Give the explorers and routes quiz. Check before moving on: ask "First circumnavigation?" Look for: Magellan's expedition (1519–1522), completed by Elcano.

questions.a: Magellan's expedition (1519–1522), completed by Elcano.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: motives, technologies, Dias 1488, da Gama 1498, Columbus 1492, Magellan 1519–22, Cabrillo 1542. Map: routes labeled.

weeks.prep: Foods from the Columbian Exchange; Equiano excerpt (preview: describes the Middle Passage's brutality); trade simulation cards.
misconceptions: Thinking the exchange was equal. Disease devastated Indigenous Americans.
Thinking mercantilism means free trade.

days.guide: Sort foods, animals and diseases. Check before moving on: ask "From the Americas?" Look for: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco.

questions.a: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco.
Horses, cattle, wheat, sugar cane, smallpox.

days.guide: Analyze population data. Check before moving on: ask "Impact of disease?" Look for: Native population fell by as much as 90% in some areas.

questions.a: Native population fell by as much as 90% in some areas.

days.guide: Read Equiano. Check before moving on: ask "Middle Passage?" Look for: Voyage from Africa to Americas: crowded, chained, disease, high death rates.

questions.a: Voyage from Africa to Americas: crowded, chained, disease, high death rates.

days.guide: Play the mercantilism simulation. Your child explains joint-stock companies and market economies. Check before moving on: ask "Mercantilism?" Look for: Colonies supply raw materials and buy finished goods to enrich the mother country.

questions.a: Colonies supply raw materials and buy finished goods to enrich the mother country.
Investors share costs and profits (Dutch East India Company).

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph on the most significant effect of the Columbian Exchange. Check before moving on: ask "Candidate answer?" Look for: Disease — largest population effect.

questions.a: Disease — largest population effect.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence answering the prompt, at least two accurate specific facts or document references, explanation of how they support the claim, concluding sentence; 3 = accurate but thin explanation; 2 = general statements, few facts; 1 = off-topic or inaccurate. Simulation reflection: explains mercantilism and joint-stock companies accurately.

weeks.prep: Locke's Second Treatise excerpt; Montesquieu excerpt; costumes or name cards for salon.
misconceptions: Thinking Enlightenment thinkers all agreed.
Thinking separation of powers is the same as federalism.

days.guide: Your child creates a flowchart linking Greek, Roman, Christian, Renaissance, Reformation and Scientific Revolution ideas to the Enlightenment. Check before moving on: ask "Scientific Revolution's link?" Look for: Reason and natural laws could apply to society.

questions.a: Reason and natural laws could apply to society.

days.guide: Read Locke's Second Treatise excerpts. Your child explains natural rights in their own words. Check before moving on: ask "Natural rights?" Look for: Life, liberty and property.

questions.a: Life, liberty and property.
People may change or overthrow it.

days.guide: Read Montesquieu on separation of powers. Your child diagrams three branches with checks. Check before moving on: ask "Three branches?" Look for: Legislative, executive, judicial — to prevent tyranny.

questions.a: Legislative, executive, judicial — to prevent tyranny.

days.guide: Role-play a salon among Locke, Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu; your child plays two roles. Check before moving on: ask "Voltaire's ideas?" Look for: Freedom of speech and religion.

questions.a: Freedom of speech and religion.
Social contract, general will.

days.guide: Give the Enlightenment thinkers quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Locke's work?" Look for: Two Treatises of Government (1689).

questions.a: Two Treatises of Government (1689).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: Locke natural rights, Montesquieu separation of powers, Voltaire free speech, Rousseau social contract. Salon rubric: accurate views, interaction.

weeks.prep: Magna Carta, English Bill of Rights, Declaration of Independence (National Archives); five DBQ documents.
misconceptions: Thinking the Declaration created the government. It declared independence; the Constitution created the government.
Thinking democracy ideas came only from America.

days.guide: Read key clauses of the 1689 English Bill of Rights. Your child compares them with Magna Carta in a chart. Check before moving on: ask "Key protections?" Look for: No taxes without Parliament, free elections, no cruel and unusual punishment.

questions.a: No taxes without Parliament, free elections, no cruel and unusual punishment.

days.guide: Read the Declaration's preamble. Your child highlights Locke's ideas. Check before moving on: ask "Locke's ideas?" Look for: Unalienable rights, consent of the governed, right to alter or abolish government.

questions.a: Unalienable rights, consent of the governed, right to alter or abolish government.

days.guide: Your child plans the DBQ essay using 5 documents: thesis, document groupings and outline. Check before moving on: ask "Thesis example?" Look for: Limits on rulers, protection of rights and consent of the governed built over 1215–1776.

questions.a: Limits on rulers, protection of rights and consent of the governed built over 1215–1776.

days.guide: Your child writes the DBQ essay with a thesis and evidence from each document. Check before moving on: ask "Each paragraph?" Look for: Topic sentence, document evidence, explanation.

questions.a: Topic sentence, document evidence, explanation.

days.guide: Your child revises and submits the DBQ essay. Check before moving on: ask "What to check?" Look for: Thesis, all documents used, citations.

questions.a: Thesis, all documents used, citations.

weeks.assessment_key: DBQ rubric: thesis, evidence from all 5 documents, chronological development, explanation, conventions.

weeks.prep: Year timeline; review cards; final exam.
misconceptions: Memorizing dates without connections.
Ignoring maps.

days.guide: Your child traces one theme (trade, religion or government) across all nine units on a chart. Check before moving on: ask "Trade example?" Look for: Silk Road, gold-salt, Columbian Exchange.

questions.a: Silk Road, gold-salt, Columbian Exchange.

days.guide: Your child completes the wall timeline and quizzes themself on 30 key events and dates. Check before moving on: ask "476?" Look for: Fall of Western Rome.

questions.a: Fall of Western Rome.

days.guide: Review unit study guides with flashcards and map practice. Check before moving on: ask "Locate Timbuktu." Look for: Niger River, Mali.

questions.a: Niger River, Mali.

days.guide: Give the year-end world history exam with a map section and short essay. Check before moving on: ask "1517?" Look for: 95 Theses.

questions.a: 95 Theses.

days.guide: Your child writes and presents a reflection on which civilization or idea most shaped today's world. Check before moving on: ask "Strong reflection?" Look for: Specific civilization or idea with evidence.

questions.a: Specific civilization or idea with evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam: map section; key dates (476, 622, 1054, 1215, 1324, 1347, 1453, 1492, 1517, 1521, 1687, 1776); short essay with thesis and evidence.
